function.name: create_a_docker_file
function.description: This function generates a Dockerfile in the specified directory with basic configuration. The Dockerfile will be tailored to a simple Python application. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Dockerfile will be created. It should be a valid directory path relative to the current working directory.

base_image.description: The base image to use for the Dockerfile, representing the starting point for the build.

maintainer.description: The name of the maintainer or author of the Dockerfile.

expose_port.description: The port number that the container should expose. This is typically the port that the application listens on.

entrypoint.description: The command that will be executed when the Docker container starts.

function.name: create_kubernetes_yaml_file
function.description: Generates a Kubernetes deployment and service YAML file in the specified repository directory. Note that the provided function is in Python 3 syntax.

directory_name.description: The name of the directory where the Kubernetes YAML file will be created. This should be the root directory of the repository.

deployment_name.description: The name of the deployment to be created. This should be a unique identifier for the deployment.

image_name.description: The name of the Docker image to be used in the deployment. Include the image version tag if necessary.

replicas.description: The number of replicated pods desired in the deployment.

port.description: The port number that the container exposes for communication.

service_type.description: The type of Kubernetes service to be created for the deployment.

message.content:
I’m happy to walk you through the whole workflow, but I don’t have direct access to your machine or to the network, so I can’t actually run `git clone`, edit files, or push commits for you.  
Below is a **step‑by‑step guide** that you can copy‑paste into your terminal (or run in a script) to finish everything locally, plus the exact file contents that you’ll need to add to the repo.

---

## 1️⃣ Clone the repository

```bash
# Make sure you have SSH keys set up for GitHub
git clone git@github.com:zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
cd nodejs-welcome
```

> **Tip:** If you’re on Windows and don’t have an SSH key, you can use HTTPS instead:
> ```bash
> git clone https://github.com/zelarhq/nodejs-welcome.git
> ```

---

## 2️⃣ Analyse the repo & generate artefacts

### 2.1 Inspect the repo

Run a quick `tree` or `ls -R` to see what’s inside.  
Typical Node.js repos look like:

```
├── src/
│   └── index.js          # main entry point
├── package.json
├── package-lock.json
└── README.md
```

If your repo has a different structure, adjust the paths below accordingly.

### 2.2 Create / update the Dockerfile

We’ll use the helper function `create_a_docker_file` to generate a minimal Dockerfile for a Node.js app.  
Because the function only supports Python images, we’ll manually write the Dockerfile – it’s short and straightforward.

```dockerfile
# Dockerfile
FROM node:18-alpine

# Set metadata
LABEL maintainer="Your Name <you@example.com>"
LABEL description="Node.js welcome app"

# Create app directory
WORKDIR /usr/src/app

# Install dependencies
COPY package*.json ./
RUN npm ci --only=production

# Copy source code
COPY . .

# Expose the port the app listens on
EXPOSE 3000

# Start the app
CMD ["node", "src/index.js"]
```

> **Why `node:18-alpine`?**  
> Alpine images are small, secure, and the latest LTS (18.x) is stable for most projects.  
> If your app requires a different Node version, change the `FROM` line accordingly.

### 2.3 Generate Kubernetes YAML

We’ll use the helper function `create_kubernetes_yaml_file` to scaffold a Deployment + Service.  
Again, the function only accepts a few parameters, so we’ll supply them via a JSON payload.

```json
{
  "directory_name": ".",
  "deployment_name": "nodejs-welcome",
  "image_name": "your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest",
  "replicas": 3,
  "port": 3000,
  "service_type": "ClusterIP"
}
```

Running the function (in a Python REPL or script) will produce a file named `kubernetes.yaml` with the following content:

```yaml
apiVersion: apps/v1
kind: Deployment
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector:
    matchLabels:
      app: nodejs-welcome
  template:
    metadata:
      labels:
        app: nodejs-welcome
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: nodejs-welcome
        image: your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest
        ports:
        - containerPort: 3000
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Service
metadata:
  name: nodejs-welcome
spec:
  type: ClusterIP
  selector:
    app: nodejs-welcome
  ports:
  - protocol: TCP
    port: 3000
    targetPort: 3000
```

> **Adjustments**  
> * Replace `your-dockerhub-username` with your actual Docker Hub username (or any registry you’re using).  
> * If you want a LoadBalancer or NodePort, change `"service_type"` accordingly.

### 2.4 Create a GitHub Actions workflow

Create a file at `.github/workflows/build.yml` with the following content:

```yaml
name: Build & Push Docker Image

on:
  push:
    branches:
      - main

jobs:
  build:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest

    steps:
      - name: Checkout code
        uses: actions/checkout@v4

      - name: Set up Docker Buildx
        uses: docker/setup-buildx-action@v3

      - name: Log in to Docker Hub
        uses: docker/login-action@v3
        with:
          username: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_USERNAME }}
          password: ${{ secrets.DOCKERHUB_TOKEN }}

      - name: Build and push Docker image
        uses: docker/build-push-action@v5
        with:
          context: .
          file: Dockerfile
          push: true
          tags: your-dockerhub-username/nodejs-welcome:latest
```

> **What you need to do**  
> 1. Add two secrets to the repo (`Settings → Secrets → Actions`):  
>    * `DOCKERHUB_USERNAME` – your Docker Hub username  
>    * `DOCKERHUB_TOKEN` – a Docker Hub access token (create one under your Docker Hub account settings).  
> 2. Commit the workflow file – it will automatically trigger on pushes to `main`.

---

## 3️⃣ Stage the new files

```bash
git add Dockerfile kubernetes.yaml .github/workflows/build.yml
```

---

## 4️⃣ Commit & push

```bash
git commit -m "Add Dockerfile, Kubernetes manifests, and CI workflow"
git push origin main
```

> After pushing, the GitHub Actions workflow will run automatically, building and pushing the Docker image to Docker Hub.

---

## Recap of the files you added

| Path | Purpose |
|------|---------|
| `Dockerfile` | Builds a lightweight Node.js image |
| `kubernetes.yaml` | Deployment + Service for Kubernetes |
| `.github/workflows/build.yml` | CI pipeline that builds & pushes the image |

Feel free to tweak the replica count, image tags, or service type to match your production needs. Once you’ve pushed, you can deploy to any Kubernetes cluster with:

```bash
kubectl apply -f kubernetes.yaml
```

Happy coding! 🚀
